reasoning_traces.think:
The foundational structure of probability theory emerges from the interplay between Boolean σ-algebras and numerical measures. Starting with a sample space Ω, we define a σ-algebra F of subsets representing possible events. Each event E ∈ F can be interpreted as a proposition about outcomes. A probability measure μ assigns values in [0,1] to these events, satisfying countable additivity and normalization. In the die-rolling example, each En corresponds to a specific outcome sequence ending in 6 on the nth roll. The union ∪En captures all finite termination scenarios, forming a complete event E. This construction ensures that E has well-defined probability μ(E), which converges to 1 due to geometric series behavior. The dual event E'—representing infinite non-termination—is logically valid but practically negligible. The measure μ thus bridges qualitative event logic with quantitative inference, enabling both Bayesian updating and GSE-based dynamic reasoning.
